reader.summary: During the reporting window, North Korea's most prominent development was the official opening of the New Yalu River Bridge linking the country to China, a project delayed for twelve years. State media confirmed the ceremony, and trucks bearing Chinese flags were photographed crossing into Sinuiju. Analysts noted the bridge may help Pyongyang route trade through China and partially offset sanctions pressure, though some experts cautioned that near-term volumes would remain modest. In parallel, North Korea conducted a series of submarine-launched missile tests, including an AI-equipped torpedo and two types of cruise missiles fired from a sub — the first underwater-launched missile exercises in nearly three years. State media released imagery of the launches. North Korea's missile chief publicly questioned South Korea's recent hypersonic glide vehicle test, underscoring the ongoing arms rivalry. Domestically, a report highlighted growing food shortages as drought threatened crops. Satellite imagery also offered a rare glimpse of Kim Jong Un's summer retreat. The week combined a major diplomatic-economic milestone with a reminder of Pyongyang's expanding maritime missile capability.

display.eli5:
North Korea just opened a big new bridge to China after waiting twelve years. Next week, news will focus on whether trucks actually carry much cargo across it, and whether that really helps North Korea dodge the trade rules other countries set for it.

At the same time, North Korea fired cruise missiles from under the sea, and its missile boss picked a fight with South Korea over a fancy new missile Seoul tested. Expect South Korea and Japan to respond with formal statements, and North Korea to push back with another strong declaration tying the tests together.

On top of that, the crops are drying up because of a long drought. As harvest time wraps up, expect more reports about food running low and the government having to adjust rations or declare emergency grain measures.

The satellite photos of Kim Jong Un's summer hideout are a one-off story and will vanish from the news. The bigger surprise nobody is expecting: a back-channel hint that a North Korea-United States meeting might actually be getting scheduled.
